title: How an AI agent on a developer-tools website tells a stuck developer from a buyer
summary: Support questions get the weakest answers on developer-tools sites. Storylane Buyability Index data on how an AI agent should sort developers from buyers.
body_markdown:
Put a chat agent on a developer-tools website and the first worry is that it turns into a support desk. Someone pastes an error, someone asks why a deploy failed, someone wants to reset an API key. The fear is real, but I think it points at the smaller risk. The bigger one runs the other way: on a developer-tools site, a buyer's question often sounds like a support question, and an agent tuned to send support questions away sends the buyer away too.


So the agent's first job is not answering. It is sorting. Is this a developer who is stuck, or a buyer who is checking whether they can rely on you? Each deserves a fast, good answer, and the two answers go to different places.


## What does the data say about developer-tools websites?


The Storylane Buyability Index scanned 529 B2B websites between Sep 8 and Oct 20, 2026, and checked 20 buyer questions per site, 10,580 in all. Two caveats belong next to every number from it. The questions were generated per company (what a buyer would plausibly ask), not logged from real buyers. And the sites were chosen by the people who ran the scans, so this is not a random sample of the web.


For this piece I picked out the 29 sites in the index that sell developer tools: developer platforms, APIs, databases, hosting and code tools. That is my own hand classification, and it gives 580 questions. Here is how those sites compare with the other 500.


Question 29 developer-tools sites 500 other sites


Questions answered in full 71% (409 of 580) 58% (5,795 of 10,000)


Product and integration questions answered in full 89% (129 of 145) 74% (2,090 of 2,819)


Support, pricing, ROI and implementation questions answered in full 57% (153 of 270) 46% (2,160 of 4,672)


Support questions answered in full 45% (27 of 60) 44% (466 of 1,067)


Questions from technical buyers answered in full 77% (272 of 354) 62% (2,105 of 3,373)


Questions from executives answered in full 57% (133 of 232) 52% (2,298 of 4,405)


Full answers that came from docs or developer pages 41% (169 of 409) 8% (461 of 5,795)


Developer-tools sites answer more than the rest of the index, and they answer the person building with the product best of all. The weak spot is the same one everyone has, only more visible next to the strengths: support was the worst-answered of the main topics on these 29 sites, and the gap between what a technical buyer can find (77%) and what an executive can find (57%) is about 20 points, nearly twice the 10-point gap on the other sites.


## Why do support questions get the weakest answers?


Look at what "support" means in these questions. The index generates buyer questions by design, so none of them is "my build is broken". They read like this: what uptime SLA do enterprise customers get, what support channels exist if we hit a production incident, how fast are response times, is there a named contact. On the developer-tools sites, 44 questions mentioned SLAs, uptime, incidents or response times, and 14 of them (32%) got a full answer.


Those are not support requests. They are purchase questions wearing support words. The person asking is deciding whether to put your product in the path of something that matters, and they want to know what happens on the bad day.


I have a theory for why these go unanswered on sites that answer everything else. The obvious explanation is that companies hide SLAs on purpose, to keep them for negotiation. That fits some of it. But it does not explain why these sites answer pricing and security so much better. I think the real reason is who writes the site. Developer-tools companies write for the builder, and the builder's questions live in the docs, which engineers keep current because they use them. Support terms live in contracts and in the heads of the sales and success teams. Nobody's job is to put them on a page, so they end up on no page.


The docs pull even buying answers toward them. Of the 53 pricing questions these sites answered in full, 25 were answered from docs or developer pages and 18 from the pricing page. The homepage supplied one full answer out of 409. On a developer-tools site, the buyer is reading the docs too. There is more on that pattern in[why most B2B websites answer buyer questions in the docs, not on the homepage](https://www.storylane.io/blog/website-answers-hidden-in-docs) .


## The now-or-later test


If a buyer's question sounds like support and a support question shows up on the docs page where buyers also read, the agent needs a better rule than topic or page. The one I would use is simple:


**A question about something broken now is support. A question about what happens when something breaks later is a purchase.**


A stuck developer talks about the present and about themselves: my key, my build, this error, it stopped working. A buyer talks about the future and about the organisation: our team, enterprise, contract, what happens if, how fast will you respond. Both may use the words "support" and "incident". The tense gives them away.


The examples below are illustrative, written to show the shape of each kind of question, not taken from real chats.


Stuck developer (now) Buyer (later)


My webhook stopped firing after I rotated the key. What do I check? If a webhook outage hits our production traffic, how fast does your team respond?


Why is my deploy hitting a rate limit on the free plan? What rate limits apply on an enterprise contract, and can they be raised?


How do I add a teammate to my project? Do enterprise accounts get a named contact or a shared queue?


Is there a status page? The API is returning 500s. What uptime SLA do you put in writing, and what are the credits if you miss it?


The test is not perfect. A developer at a large company may ask a "later" question because their manager asked them to. That is fine: then they are acting as a buyer, and the question should be treated as one.


## How should the agent route each one?


The two answers have little in common, which is why the sort matters.


### The stuck developer: answer, link, get out of the way


- Answer from the docs and link the exact page. On these sites the answer usually exists: docs supplied 41% of every full answer.
- Do not ask qualifying questions or for a work email. A developer with a failing build reads that as a toll booth.
- Offer the real support path (status page, support ticket, community) when the docs do not solve it.
- Keep these conversations out of the lead list. A stuck free-plan user logged as a sales lead pollutes the pipeline and wastes a rep's morning.


### The buyer: answer what you can, then hand over with context


- Answer the parts that are public: support tiers, the published SLA, security pages. Partial answers were the most common outcome for support questions on these sites (32 of 60), so the agent should say what is known and be plain about what needs a person.
- Ask one or two questions that matter for the deal: team size, what they would run on you, the timeline.
- Route to an account executive with the conversation attached, so nobody asks the buyer the same question twice.
- Expect these buyers on docs pages, not only on the pricing page.


The same idea, applied to who is asking rather than what tense they use, is in[why website chat should work out who is asking before it answers](https://www.storylane.io/blog/route-partner-mssp-customer-website-chat) . And if your product has a free plan, the first minutes after signup are a third case worth its own rules: see[the free trial signup routing playbook](https://www.storylane.io/blog/route-qualify-trial-signups) .


## Isn't it simpler to split by page?


The strongest objection is that you do not need a sorting test at all. Put a support bot on the docs, a sales agent on the pricing page, and let the page decide. It is a good first step and I would do it. Page is the cheapest signal you have.


It is not enough on its own, for the reason in the data above: buyers on developer-tools sites read the docs. Nearly half of the full pricing answers on these 29 sites came from docs pages. A buyer who lands on your API reference and asks about uptime commitments is exactly the person a docs-only support bot will send to a ticket form. The page sets the default. The question decides the route.


There is a second reason. The buying questions on these sites are the weakest-answered ones, and that is not specific to developer tools: across the whole index, the questions that decide a deal get worse answers than the easy ones (more in[B2B websites answer 69% of easy buyer questions and only 50% of the ones that decide the deal](https://www.storylane.io/blog/b2b-website-assurance-gap) ). An agent that can tell a "later" question from a "now" question is the cheapest way to catch the buyer at the exact moment the site runs out of answers.


## Where an AI sales agent fits


I run marketing at Storylane, and we sell an AI website agent, RepX, so weigh this section with that in mind.


RepX is built for this kind of split. Each page gets its own playbook, with its own starter prompts, calls to action and calendar, so the pricing page can book an account executive while the docs page books support. Qualification questions are set per page and asked in conversation rather than through a form. Guardrails set what the agent will and will not say about pricing, competitors and compliance. Qualified leads and conversation summaries flow to HubSpot, Salesforce and Slack. It is best for developer-tools teams whose website already has good docs and who want the buyers reading those docs to reach a person while they are still interested.


If your buyers also arrive from AI search with a shortlist already open, the same sorting applies at the first message. I covered that in[can your website answer a buyer who arrived from ChatGPT?](https://www.storylane.io/blog/website-answer-buyer-from-chatgpt)


## What to do on Monday


Pull your last 100 chat conversations. Tag each one "now" or "later" using the test above. Then check two things for the "later" ones: which page they started on, and where they ended up. If buyers asking about SLAs, response times and enterprise support ended in a ticket form or a docs link, you have found pipeline your site is turning away. Then write down your support terms on one public page, so the agent has something to answer from.


The one idea to keep: on a developer-tools site, the words do not tell you who is buying. The tense does.
